primary_sources.source: ISO/IEC 25010:2023, Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE) — Product quality model
primary_sources.relevance: The current product-quality model defines nine characteristics and their subcharacteristics for specifying, measuring, and evaluating ICT products. ISO expressly positions the model for requirements, test objectives, quality-control criteria, and acceptance criteria. It supports a traceable quality matrix, but the public abstract does not supply project-specific metrics or thresholds.

Defines a general data-quality model for structured data in computer systems. Its inherent and system-dependent quality perspective supports evaluating disaster records for qualities such as accuracy, completeness, consistency, credibility, currentness, accessibility, availability, portability, recoverability, and traceability, subject to access to the normative standard and selection of context-appropriate measures.

primary_sources.source: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, Recommendation
primary_sources.relevance: Provides technology-neutral, testable success criteria organized under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust principles. Level AA requires satisfaction of all Level A and AA criteria for complete pages; conformance does not cover every disability-related need and requires accessibility-supported implementations, including assistive-technology testing.

primary_sources.source: Brooke, J. (1996), SUS: A quick and dirty usability scale
primary_sources.relevance: Introduces the ten-item System Usability Scale and its 0–100 scoring transformation. SUS is a post-use perceived-usability measure whose interpretation depends on a specified system, users, tasks, and context; it does not directly measure task accuracy, accessibility, information quality, operational effectiveness, or disaster outcomes.

primary_sources.source: Mehta, Bruns, and Newton (2017), Trust, but verify: social media models for disaster management
primary_sources.relevance: A multi-year empirical project combining social-media analysis, observation inside an emergency-management organization, and stakeholder engagement. It identifies information gathering, quasi-journalistic verification, and crowdsourcing models and shows that source/content verification, trust, power, and responsibility must be explicit when user-generated information informs decisions.

primary_sources.source: Haworth et al. (2018), The Good, the Bad, and the Uncertain: Contributions of Volunteered Geographic Information to Community Disaster Resilience
primary_sources.relevance: Synthesizes evidence that volunteered geographic information may be partial and skewed because access, skills, demographics, geography, and participation are unequal. It cautions that marginalized and disaster-vulnerable people can be absent from maps, supporting representation audits and non-digital reporting channels rather than assuming the crowd represents the affected population.

primary_sources.source: Yan et al. (2020), The representativeness and spatial bias of volunteered geographic information: a review
primary_sources.relevance: Distinguishes demographic bias in who contributes from spatial bias in what locations are observed. Opportunistic VGI collection does not guarantee representativeness, so volume, map coverage, or model accuracy on contributed reports cannot alone establish population coverage or equitable service.

primary_sources.source: Rizza et al. (2020), Decision support for medical disasters: Evaluation of the IMPRESS system in the live Palermo demo
primary_sources.relevance: Reports evaluation through table-top and live multi-agency exercises using predefined KPIs, external expert evaluators, observers, user questionnaires, and debriefing. It supports controlled scenario testing with recorded inputs and observable outputs, while one demonstration cannot establish effectiveness across all hazards or jurisdictions.

primary_sources.source: NIST Technical Note 2086, A Review of Social Media Use During Disaster Response and Recovery Phases
primary_sources.relevance: A government technical review finds potential situational-awareness value alongside information overload, quality, privacy, and integration challenges. It supports human verification and workflow evaluation, not automatic treatment of social-media content as authoritative evidence.

evidence.evidence_quality_and_caveats: ISO and W3C are authoritative consensus standards, not empirical proof that this particular product improves disaster outcomes. Full normative ISO text may require licensed access; claims should cite only provisions actually consulted. SUS is an original instrument for perceived usability, not a percentage score or a standalone pass/fail test. The disaster-information studies span different countries, platforms, hazards, and organizational settings; their findings justify design controls and hypotheses but do not determine Zamboanga City effect sizes. Literature on VGI and social media is especially vulnerable to platform, language, connectivity, demographic, and spatial selection effects. A prototype evaluation can establish conformance, data-quality performance on a defined test set, usability in defined tasks, and comparative workflow performance; it cannot establish reduced casualties, citywide preparedness, or superior real-disaster decisions without longitudinal or operational evidence. Report sample frames, missing data, confidence intervals, protocol deviations, and negative results, and distinguish simulated from operational evidence.

paper_implications.scope_inclusions: Include information-quality controls across the paper's actual submodules: source attribution and provenance; verification status (unverified, corroborated, verified, rejected, superseded); timestamps and currentness; location precision; duplicate/version handling; completeness rules for required fields; validation and correction history; and role-based publication. Include stakeholder-visible accessibility for keyboard and assistive-technology users, plain-language and multilingual content where validated with intended users, low-bandwidth views, and an assisted/offline intake path. Include representative test scenarios covering routine preparedness, rapidly changing incident information, conflicting reports, stale records, inaccessible attachments, duplicate reports, partial connectivity, and recovery/export. Actors should include authorized government/customer reviewers, startup support/security personnel, community contributors or informants where applicable, and intended end users including people with disabilities and limited connectivity.
paper_implications.scope_exclusions_and_dependencies: Exclude claims that the platform predicts disasters, independently verifies ground truth, replaces official warning channels or incident command, guarantees WCAG conformance through automated scanning alone, or represents the entire affected population from crowdsourced/digital data. Exclude casualty reduction and operational response-time improvement as demonstrated outcomes unless a suitably powered operational study measures them. Depend on customer-defined authoritative sources, reviewer availability, identity and access administration, connectivity and hosting, validated language translations, assistive-technology/user testing, and lawful access to reference datasets. Data quality is fitness for a stated use, not an intrinsic guarantee; incomplete source populations and offline residents remain outside a digital sample unless deliberately reached.
objective_requirements_and_metrics: Create a requirements-to-test matrix mapping each implemented submodule to applicable ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics, ISO/IEC 25012 data-quality properties, and WCAG 2.2 Level A/AA success criteria; acceptance is zero unresolved critical failures and documented disposition of every applicable requirement. Do not claim formal ISO certification unless independently obtained.

Build a frozen, versioned scenario corpus with known expected records and decisions: valid, incomplete, contradictory, duplicate, stale, mislocated, malicious, and later-corrected reports across the hazards and workflows in scope. Separate development and evaluation cases and publish the case counts, expected outputs, scoring rules, and seed/version.

For each data-quality rule calculate completeness = required populated fields / required fields; validity = values satisfying declared format/domain rules / evaluated values; duplicate detection precision = true duplicate flags / all duplicate flags; duplicate recall = true duplicate flags / all known duplicates; provenance coverage = records with source, actor, timestamp, and change history / evaluated records; and currentness compliance = records meeting the customer-defined age limit / records subject to that limit. Report numerator, denominator, confidence interval where appropriate, and error examples.

Measure verification performance separately from ingestion speed: sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, and confusion matrix against an independently adjudicated reference set. Preserve an explicit unverified state. Acceptance thresholds must be agreed with the customer from consequences of false acceptance and false rejection before testing, not selected after observing results.

Run the same scripted tasks on the current baseline workflow and prototype, counterbalancing order where feasible. Measure task completion, critical-error rate, time on task from a defined start/end, number of handoffs, and time from report receipt to reviewer-approved publication. Report paired differences and uncertainty; improvement means a pre-registered practically important difference without an unacceptable rise in critical errors.

Administer the original ten-item SUS only after participants perform representative tasks; calculate the standard 0–100 SUS score, report distribution and confidence interval, and compare with a declared baseline or published norm cautiously. Do not label SUS as a percentage or infer operational effectiveness from it.

Test every in-scope page and state against WCAG 2.2 Level AA using automated checks plus manual keyboard, focus, zoom/reflow, labels/name-role-value, error identification, contrast, and assistive-technology checks. Acceptance requires all applicable A and AA criteria for full pages; log tester, browser, assistive technology, language, evidence, and exceptions.

Evaluate inclusion by stratified task results rather than aggregate averages alone: report completion and error rates by relevant participant/access group, device, connection condition, language, and channel when sample sizes permit; otherwise report counts descriptively and mark the study underpowered. Test low-bandwidth and connectivity-loss recovery under reproducible network profiles.

Conduct at least one table-top exercise with government/customer personnel using injected conflicts, outage, correction, and escalation events. Score correct routing, acknowledgement latency, provenance retained, inappropriate disclosure, recovery time, and decisions consistent with the approved protocol; use independent observers and a structured debrief.

Use a pre-specified severity scheme: critical means potential unauthorized disclosure, corruption/loss, publication of rejected information as verified, inability to complete a safety-critical task, or an accessibility barrier blocking that task. Record all defects and retest fixes. Avoid a single composite quality score that can hide a critical failure.
paper_implications.significance_mechanisms_and_beneficiarie: Government/customer personnel may benefit when structured provenance, status, and review workflows reduce search, duplication, and ambiguity; community and partner organizations may benefit when approved information is more current, traceable, accessible, and available through multiple channels; the startup may benefit from reusable quality evidence, support procedures, and accountable service boundaries. These are conditional mechanisms, not guaranteed outcomes: they require accurate source data, timely reviewers, adoption, training, accessible interfaces, connectivity alternatives, and integration with official procedures. Possible harms include amplifying false or stale reports, excluding offline or underrepresented groups, revealing sensitive locations or identities, automation bias, and false confidence from aggregate metrics. Claim stakeholder or operational significance only when baseline-comparative task results, accessibility evidence, quality error rates, and exercise observations support the specific causal link; reserve public-safety outcome claims for real operational or longitudinal evaluation with appropriate controls.

governance_and_design.authority_and_responsibility_matrix: Government/customer: define authoritative sources, data meanings, risk tolerances, verification protocol, publishing authority, accessibility and language needs, retention instructions, and incident decisions; appoint reviewers and approve/reject/correct records. Startup: implement and document controls, preserve provenance and audit logs, operate hosting/support within contract, remediate defects, provide exports, disclose incidents, and never represent unverified content as officially approved. Shared: approve scenario tests, adjudicate reference data, conduct accessibility/user exercises, review metrics, manage changes, and document residual risk. Community contributors supply observations but do not acquire official approval authority merely by contributing. Independent evaluators should adjudicate benchmark truth and observe high-stakes exercises where feasible. Every displayed status must identify who asserted it, when, under which rule/version, and whether it is official approval or system validation only.
governance_and_design.data_lifecycle_and_interoperability: At capture, assign a stable identifier and retain source/channel, contributor or accountable actor as lawful, event and ingestion timestamps, location with precision, consent/use restrictions, and original content hash where appropriate. Classify sensitivity and verification state; validate schema without conflating syntactic validity with truth. During review, keep append-only status/change events, corroborating evidence links, reviewer identity, reasons, and timestamps. Published corrections should supersede rather than silently overwrite prior assertions. Use documented schemas, controlled vocabularies, time zone/coordinate reference system, machine-readable export, and stable identifiers; version schema and validation rules. Quality dashboards must expose denominators and missingness. Retention, archival, deletion, and legal-hold decisions belong to the customer/controller under applicable policy; the startup executes documented instructions. On contract exit provide tested, documented export plus audit metadata and securely dispose of residual copies after authorized confirmation, subject to legal obligations.
governance_and_design.risk_continuity_and_inclusion: Apply least privilege, tenant isolation, encryption, protected audit logs, backup/restore tests, incident response, dependency inventory, and recovery objectives agreed with the customer. Prevent cross-tenant search, cache, export, analytics, and support access; test these boundaries. Minimize personal and precise-location data, restrict sensitive fields, and assess re-identification before release. Cache or queue safe drafts during connectivity loss, show synchronization state, prevent duplicate submissions, and provide a non-digital/assisted route rather than treating app non-use as absence of need. Target WCAG 2.2 AA with manual and assistive-technology testing, accessible authentication, visible focus, adequate target size, non-drag alternatives, redundant-entry avoidance, consistent help, captions/text alternatives, and error recovery. Recruit intended users including disability, age, language, device, and low-connectivity perspectives; track who is missing from testing and incoming data. Compare geographic/demographic contribution coverage with an appropriate population or hazard-exposure denominator where lawful, but never infer representativeness from report volume. Maintain provider-exit exports, restore drills, fallback contact procedures, and an official-channel banner during outages.
